title: The Collection, Travel Plans, and Final Greetings
summary: Paul gives instructions for the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem, asking each person to set aside money on the first day of every week. He shares his travel plans, commends Timothy, explains Apollos's delay, and urges the church to honor faithful workers like Stephanas. He closes with greetings from Asia, a line in his own hand, a warning, the Aramaic prayer “Come, O Lord,” and a word of love.
story: After the soaring end of chapter 15, the letter lands in practical business, and the transition is deliberate: 15:58 had just told the church that their labor in the Lord is not in vain. Chapter 16 shows what that labor looks like: giving money for strangers, receiving and supporting workers, and keeping the church's relationships in good repair. The collection mentioned briefly here becomes a major theme of 2 Corinthians 8 and 9 and of Paul's last visit to Jerusalem (Romans 15:25-28; Acts 24:17). His travel plans, which later changed, became a sore point, as 2 Corinthians 1 will show.
historical:
Paul writes from Ephesus, the leading city of the Roman province of Asia (in western modern Turkey), where he spent more than two years (Acts 19:10). He plans to stay until Pentecost, the Jewish feast fifty days after Passover, then travel through Macedonia (northern Greece) to Corinth, possibly spending the winter there, when sea travel largely stopped. Acts 19 describes the “great door” and the opposition (verse 9) in Ephesus, including a riot provoked by silversmiths whose trade in images of the goddess Artemis was threatened.

The collection was a relief fund for the Christians in Jerusalem, many of them poor, and Paul had agreed with the Jerusalem leaders to remember the poor (Galatians 2:10). He organized it among the Gentile churches of Galatia, Macedonia, and Achaia. Aquila and Prisca (Priscilla), a Jewish Christian couple who had worked with Paul in Corinth after the emperor Claudius expelled Jews from Rome (Acts 18:2), were now in Ephesus and hosted a church in their home.
cultural:
Letters in the Roman world were usually dictated to a trained scribe, and the author often added a closing line in his own handwriting as a mark of authenticity, as Paul does in verse 21. The holy kiss (verse 20) was a common greeting among family members and close friends, and Christians used it as a sign that they were one family. Travelers depended on hospitality and letters of recommendation, which is why Paul asks the church to welcome Timothy and to send delegates with letters to Jerusalem (verse 3).

The phrase translated “Come, O Lord” (verse 22) is Aramaic, maranatha, the language Jesus and the first Jerusalem believers spoke. That a Greek-speaking church knew it without translation shows it was an early prayer passed from Aramaic-speaking believers to Gentile congregations. The earliest Christians' gathering on the first day of the week (verse 2), the day of Jesus's resurrection, is also attested in Acts 20:7.
literary: The chapter follows the standard pattern of ancient letter closings: practical instructions, travel plans, commendations of associates, exhortations, greetings from others, a signature, and a farewell. Two sections open with the formula “Now about” (verses 1 and 12), the last of the answers to the Corinthians' letter. Verses 13 and 14 are a burst of five short commands ending with “Do everything in love,” a summary of the whole letter's ethic. The closing lines combine a warning (“let him be under a curse”), a prayer for Christ's return, grace, and love in a few words.

outline.t: The collection for the saints in Jerusalem
Stand firm; do everything in love

doctrines.note: Churches separated by distance and ethnicity belong to one another. Gentile believers in Greece give to Jewish believers in Jerusalem, and churches in Asia send greetings to Corinth. The collection makes visible the unity of Jew and Gentile in one body.
“Come, O Lord” (verse 22) shows that the earliest believers prayed for Christ's return, echoing the hope of chapter 15. Revelation ends with a similar prayer (Revelation 22:20).

The church meets in households (verses 15 and 19), and believers greet one another with a holy kiss. The household of Stephanas is praised for devoting itself to serving the saints, showing a whole family turned outward in service.

words.note: Logeia, collection. The word appears in papyri for collections of money, including religious contributions. Paul organizes the fund with care: regular, proportional giving, delegates chosen by the church, and letters to accompany them, so that it would be transparent and trustworthy.

Maran atha, an Aramaic phrase. Divided as maran atha it means our Lord has come; divided as marana tha it means our Lord, come, which is how the Berean Standard Bible and most translations take it. The early Christian manual called the Didache uses it in a prayer after the Lord's Supper. Its use shows that the earliest believers called Jesus Lord in prayer.

Anathema, something devoted, and here accursed, placed under God's judgment. Paul uses it for anyone who does not love the Lord (verse 22). It is a solemn warning inside a warm farewell, reminding readers that love for Christ is the heart of the faith.

Thura, door. “A great door for effective work has opened to me” (verse 9). Paul often uses the image of an open door for an opportunity to preach (2 Corinthians 2:12; Colossians 4:3). Notice that the open door came with many opponents.

christ: The letter ends with Christ at the center. “Come, O Lord” (verse 22) is addressed to Jesus, which means that within a generation of the crucifixion, Aramaic-speaking believers were praying to him as Lord and longing for his return. The warning against anyone who does not love the Lord makes love for Jesus the heart of Christian identity. The closing blessing, “The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you” (verse 23), and Paul's love for them “in Christ Jesus” (verse 24) frame everything. Even the ordinary business of the chapter (money, travel, commendations) is done “in the Lord,” showing that Christ's lordship reaches into practical affairs.
questions: Paul asked for regular, planned giving for people the Corinthians had never met. How do you decide what to give and to whom?
Paul's open door came with many opponents. How do you tell whether opposition means you should stop or keep going?
“Do everything in love” sums up the letter. What is one thing you are doing this week that needs to be done more lovingly?
